groups.summary: I reproduced all six members on Python 3.13.16 with websockets 14.1, using my own fake CDP peer and also real headless Chromium 141. Three things go wrong. (1) When Transaction.__call__ fails to parse a reply, the exception escapes Listener.listener_loop at the `tx(**message)` call, which has no try around it. The listener dies, and the Transaction it already popped from mapper is never resolved: send() hangs forever, and neither later sends nor aclose() release it. (2) An async handler whose arity is wrong raises TypeError synchronously in the callback dispatch. The code logs it and then re-raises on purpose, which kills the listener. (3) Any exception from _receive_message other than TimeoutError, CancelledError or ConnectionClosed (JSONDecodeError, KeyError, ConcurrencyError) also kills the listener without logging anything. In cases (2) and (3) the tx stays in mapper, so an in-flight send hangs until some later send() starts a new Listener. Once the browser connection's listener is dead, every send from a flat-session tab hangs: Tab.aopen/_attach_session returns early and never revives the parent's listener, so nobody reads the shared websocket.

member_verdicts.note: Fake peer sends a non-JSON text frame before the Browser.getVersion reply. Listener exc is JSONDecodeError, nothing is logged, and send stays pending after 3s with mapper=[1]. Stuck at connection.py:662 send `return await tx`. A malformed Target.detachedFromTarget with no params.sessionId gives KeyError('sessionId') from _receive_message with the same hang. A second reader on the websocket (artificial setup) kills the listener with ConcurrencyError. Refinement: the tx stays in mapper, so the hang ends at the next send() on that connection (that run printed 'original done=True result=P'). I found no natural trigger in zendriver for the ConcurrencyError or the non-JSON frame, so the triggers are defensive / low realism even though the mechanism is real.

Target.getTargetInfo answered with result={} gives listener exc KeyError('targetInfo'), mapper size 0, and send not done after 3s. The same happens for a reply with no 'result' key (KeyError('result')) and for Storage.getCookies with sameSite 'SomeFutureValue' (ValueError("'SomeFutureValue' is not a valid CookieSameSite")). A later get_version works because a new listener is created, but the original send is still pending. I did not test the claim that _inbox piles up.

Runtime.evaluate with exceptionDetails {'bogus':1} gives KeyError('exceptionId'). A custom generator doing `return j['x']` gives KeyError('x') and hangs on the fake peer. On real Chromium a tab custom generator hung 5s instead of raising KeyError('notThere'), with tab mapper size 0. A generator that yields twice reaches the explicit `raise ProtocolException('could not parse...')`, which also kills the listener. The secondary claim holds too: Connection.wait() (t=None) called while events stream stays blocked >4s at connection.py:579 `await self.listener.idle.wait()` after the bad reply kills that listener.

In all 6 parse-failure variants the send was still pending after a later successful send AND after conn.aclose() ('after aclose(): original send done=False'). The tx had been popped, so _fail_pending_transactions cannot see it. A good reply queued right behind the bad one (cmd2) also hung 3s with mapper=[2]. Zendriver logged nothing at WARNING or above.

Registering `async def bad_handler()` with zero parameters for TargetCreated, followed by a good handler, then sending a TargetCreated event before the getVersion reply: TypeError, a warning is logged, the listener dies, the good handler never fires (fired=[]), and get_version hangs 3s. The next send revives the listener and the old send completes. The next event kills the listener again ('second round' hung). Refinements: the error is logged as a warning, so it is not silent. It only applies to coroutine-function handlers. A sync handler with the wrong arity goes through asyncio.to_thread, so the error surfaces as 'Task exception was never retrieved' and the listener keeps running.

Fake peer with a SimpleNamespace owner: after the browser listener died (KeyError('nope')), two successive tab.send(Runtime.evaluate) calls each hung 3s. The tab listener was running, inbox size 0, browser listener not running, and the peer did receive the session-scoped commands. One browser-level send fixed it (value 4). Real Chromium 141 shows the same: tab.evaluate('2+2') hung 8s at tab.py:859 evaluate -> send. After browser.connection.send(get_targets()) it finished with value 4, while the browser-level tx that was lost stayed pending.

groups.summary:
I could not refute this group. Every member's mechanism reproduces on Python 3.13 and websockets 14.1, using a fake CDP peer, real headless Chromium 141, or both.

(1) Transaction.__call__ lets any non-StopIteration exception from the generated parser or a custom generator escape. The Listener.listener_loop call `tx(**message)` has no try around it, so the listener task dies. The Transaction was already popped from mapper, so its future is never resolved, and aclose()/_fail_pending_transactions cannot release it. The send() hangs permanently.

(2) In the listener_loop callback dispatch, the `raise` after logger.warning, plus the outer `except Exception: raise`, kill the listener when an async handler with the wrong arity is called.

(3) A flat-session Tab's aopen/_attach_session returns early once session_id is set. Its send() restarts only the tab's own inbox Listener. When browser.connection.listener is dead, nothing reads the shared websocket, and every tab command hangs until something sends on the browser connection.

(4) Any other exception from _receive_message (for example a JSONDecodeError) also kills the listener. I found no way for real Chrome to trigger this in the current code.

member_verdicts.note: Mechanism confirmed with a fake peer (probe_recv.py). A non-JSON text frame kills the listener with JSONDecodeError and the in-flight send hangs. The only trace is 'Task exception was never retrieved' at GC. Two refinements. (a) The tx stays in mapper, so aclose() fails it with ProtocolException('connection was closed'), and a later send() starts a new Listener that delivers replies still in the buffer. The hang is permanent only when the lost frame was itself the reply. (b) No real-Chrome trigger found. The ConcurrencyError route (the aopen race) is fixed on this branch by commit 31c92f1 (_open_lock), and I found no other way to get two concurrent recv() calls. Chrome caps reply nesting at about 300 levels (verified), below the json.loads RecursionError depth: about 976 on Python 3.11, about 9995 on 3.12/3.13. Chrome escapes lone surrogates (verified). Invalid UTF-8 becomes ConnectionClosed, which the loop already handles. Realism with real Chrome is low; a non-Chrome CDP endpoint or proxy that sends non-JSON frames could reach it.

Fake peer (probe_parse.py): Target.getTargetInfo answered with result {} -> send() hangs, listener exception KeyError('targetInfo'), mapper {}. Storage.getCookies with sameSite 'SomeFutureValue' -> ValueError and the same hang. A reply with no 'result' key -> KeyError('result') and the same hang. Other in-flight commands hang only until a later send() revives the listener: their replies are still buffered and they are still in mapper (verified in the concurrent case). The explicit raise ProtocolException('could not parse') is reachable only from a custom generator that yields twice; generated commands always end with StopIteration. On Chromium 141 with the bundled cdp, none of the 40 common command replies I tried failed to parse (verified), so the trigger needs Chrome/protocol skew. Git history shows such skew does happen: f9b442b, Chrome 146 dropped cookie sameParty and browser.cookies.get_all() broke. Note that cookies.get_all() sends on the first open tab, so that case kills only the tab listener, not the browser one.

Real Chromium (real_tab_flows.py): a custom generator returning j['notThere'] -> tab.send() hung for 5s and the tab listener died, stuck at Connection.send `return await tx`. The next tab.evaluate worked because send() restarts the tab Listener. Fake peer: KeyError from the custom generator gives the same hang. The tab.wait() sub-claim is confirmed with a fake peer (probe_wait.py): a wait() already blocked on the dead listener's idle event never returns. A new wait() does return, because its update_target send revives the listener. Realism for the custom-generator path is low to medium, since the send() docstring invites custom commands.

Fake peer: after the parse failure, conn.aclose() leaves the send pending (verified for all five parse-failure variants), because the tx was popped from mapper before tx(**message). On the browser connection this also starves every flat-session tab; see A2.4, verified with real Chrome. Parse errors in events are caught and logged (parse_json_event try/except), which shows the intended behaviour is to log and carry on. CHANGELOG entries such as 'listener crashing with InvalidStateError ... left later commands hanging forever' show maintainers treat listener death as a bug, not a design choice. No test asserts the current behaviour.

Fake peer (probe_handler.py): the listener dies only for async callables whose call raises synchronously: `async def h()`, `async def h(a,b,c)`, or functools.partial(async_f, extra). Sync functions and lambdas with the wrong arity do not kill it (they go through asyncio.to_thread and fail in their own task). Exceptions raised inside a handler body do not kill it. Neither does an instance with an async __call__ (it takes the to_thread route). Real Chromium (verified): with `async def on_request(): pass` on tab RequestWillBeSent, `tab.send(cdp.page.navigate(url))` hung for 8s, because Chrome sends the event before the navigate reply. tab.get(url) is bounded: it raises TimeoutError after 10s because of the wait_for inside Tab.get. With the same kind of handler on browser.connection for TargetInfoChanged, a tab navigation killed the browser listener. The in-flight send recovers once a later send revives the listener, but each new matching event kills it again. A warning is logged, so the user does get a hint. Realism is medium, since this is a common user mistake.

Real Chromium (real_tabs.py, verified): after the browser listener died (TypeError from a wrong-arity TargetInfoChanged handler on browser.connection), tab.evaluate('2+2') and tab.send(runtime.evaluate) each hung for 5s. The stack was at Tab.evaluate -> Connection.send `return await tx`. The tab listener was running and its inbox was empty. After `browser.connection.send(cdp.target.get_targets())` the browser listener came back and tab.evaluate returned 8. Nothing in zendriver sends on the browser connection in the background, so tabs recover only when user code makes a browser-level call (update_targets, get(new_tab=True), and so on). The browser listener does the json.loads for every frame, including those routed to sessions, so any SEED-L1 exception there also starves all tabs.

groups.summary: Confirmed: all four listener-robustness defects are real, and each needs its own fix. (1) Transaction.__call__ (connection.py ~L112-130) catches only StopIteration. A KeyError or ValueError from a generated from_json, an exception from a custom generator, or its own explicit `raise ProtocolException('could not parse...')` escapes through `tx(**message)` in Listener.listener_loop (~L973), which is outside every try. The listener dies, and the tx was already popped from mapper, so send() hangs forever and aclose() cannot release it. (2) Callback dispatch in listener_loop (~L1000-1011) logs a handler that raises when called (e.g. wrong arity) and then re-raises, which kills the listener. (3) The receive try in listener_loop catches only TimeoutError, CancelledError and ConnectionClosed. Any other exception from _receive_message (e.g. JSONDecodeError, RuntimeError/ConcurrencyError) ends the task silently and in-flight sends hang. (4) For a flat-session tab, Connection.aopen only calls _attach_session, which returns early once session_id is set. Nothing restarts the browser connection's listener, so every tab command hangs after that listener stops. The minimal local fix has 4 hunks and passes: 9 regression tests fail (hang) on the repo and pass on the prototype, on both Python 3.13 and 3.11. 68 of the repo's own tests also pass against the prototype with real headless Chromium, and mypy shows no new errors.

Use a browser-domain method (Target.getTargets) instead. (b) Severity is per path. For parse failures the tx is popped and lost, so the hang is permanent and aclose cannot release it. (c) The receive-error fix must break, not continue: a continue-based handler freezes the whole event loop on py>=3.12 when the error is persistent and synchronous (shown with ConcurrencyError). (d) Optional, not in the prototype: set self.idle on listener exit, so a wait() already blocked on the dead listener's idle event returns. This is pre-existing for ConnectionClosed too. Once hunk 1 is in, parse failures no longer kill the listener, which covers A2.3's tab.wait() side claim for that path. (e) The outer `except Exception: raise` in dispatch becomes dead code and can be dropped in the real PR.

fix_assessment.diff_summary: zendriver/core/connection.py only (full diff in Q1-fixsafety/prototype.diff). 1) Transaction.__call__: add `except Exception as e:` after `except StopIteration`, building ProtocolException('could not parse the cdp response:\n%s' % response), setting __cause__ = e, and `return self.set_exception(...)`. The trailing explicit `raise ProtocolException(...)` becomes `self.set_exception(ProtocolException(...))`. 2) Connection.aopen, flat-session branch, after `await self._attach_session(browser_connection)`: `if browser_connection.websocket is not None and (not browser_connection.listener or not browser_connection.listener.running): browser_connection.listener = Listener(browser_connection)`. 3) Listener.listener_loop receive try: add `except Exception as e:` after the ConnectionClosed clause. It logs a warning with exc_info, calls `session._fail_pending_transactions(e)` for each flat session and `self.connection._fail_pending_transactions(e)`, then `break`s; the next send() starts a new listener. 4) Listener.listener_loop callback dispatch: remove the `raise` after the per-callback logger.warning, so a faulty handler is logged and skipped.
fix_assessment.risks: No new locks, and no await between the check and the Listener() creation in hunk 2, so concurrent tab sends cannot start two readers on one websocket (no ConcurrencyError race). The check runs after _attach_lock is released, so there is no lock-ordering or re-entrancy problem. The websocket-not-None guard avoids starting a listener while the browser connection is opening (connect pending, websocket None) or after it is closed. CancelledError, KeyboardInterrupt and GeneratorExit are BaseException and stay uncaught. TimeoutError and ConnectionClosed clauses come first, so the new `except Exception` changes nothing for them. Behaviour changes callers would notice: (a) a parse failure now surfaces as ProtocolException (cause chained), not a hang. Callers that already catch ProtocolException (get_frames, _search_frames, describe_node loops, element resolve, _send_oneshot in _prepare_headless) now degrade gracefully. A custom generator that raises KeyError surfaces as ProtocolException(from KeyError), not KeyError. Setting the raw exception instead is the alternative, but it would bypass those handlers. (b) A handler that raises synchronously is logged at WARNING and the remaining handlers still run. (c) An unexpected receive error fails every in-flight command on that connection and its flat sessions with the raw exception (same style as the ConnectionClosed path). Tasks started by feed_cdp may then log 'exception never retrieved'. Replies still buffered are dropped as unknown ids when the listener restarts. Do not swap the break for continue: that freezes the event loop on py>=3.12 for persistent synchronous errors (demonstrated). Not addressed (pre-existing): a wait() already blocked on a stopped listener's idle event still hangs (setting idle on exit would fix it), and the parse-failure message embeds the full response, which may be large.

groups.summary: I tried to refute this group and could not. On real headless Chromium 141 (--headless=new, Python 3.13), a JS alert() open in the tab means DOM.getDocument and DOM.enable never get a reply. Because of that, select, find, find_all, select_all (including include_frames), xpath, wait_for, tab(...), cf_is_interactive_challenge_present and verify_cf all stay pending far past timeout=2: I watched them for 12 s, and the Chrome behaviour behind it held for more than 34 s. Nothing upstream limits the wait. Headless does not auto-dismiss the dialog. The websocket stays up (PING_TIMEOUT=900). The Target.getTargetInfo call that Connection.sleep sends does get answered, so the hang is purely in the DOM sends. The most realistic trigger is a plain script: `tab = await browser.get(page that calls alert() while loading)` returns in 0.01 s, then `await tab.select('#a', timeout=3)` hangs forever even though #a exists. Commit bd88ccd (#291) already treated exactly this 'page stuck behind a dialog' case as a bug in wait_for_ready_state, and no test asserts the current behaviour. A busy main thread that eventually finishes only makes the calls late (an 8 s busy loop made every timeout=2 call finish at about 7.6 s with the documented result); only an infinite JS loop hangs. The two side members are also real: verify_cf can run past its timeout by up to click_delay, and xpath with timeout<=0 never runs the query and otherwise spins without sleeping.

groups.refinements:
1. A true hang needs a JS dialog (alert/confirm/prompt) open in the tab, or an infinite JS loop. Bounded busy JS only overshoots until the script yields; the result is still TimeoutError, [] or False, just late.
2. The trigger is page state, not a caller argument. The most realistic path is a page that alerts during load or from a timer: browser.get/tab.get return right away (about 0.01-0.12 s, verified), and the next select/find/wait_for hangs, even for elements that exist.
3. A dialog opened by the script's own element.click() or mouse_click() hangs in that click call first (verified), so in that pattern the Q2 methods are never reached.
4. Recovery: Page.handleJavaScriptDialog returns 'No dialog is showing' unless Page.enable was sent before the dialog opened, and a late Page.enable gets no reply (verified). Navigating away with tab.get closes the dialog and DOM calls work again (verified).
5. Keepalive never ends the wait: pongs come from the browser process and PING_TIMEOUT is 900 s. Only the mechanism is assumed; the connection itself was verified still usable after 34 s, longer than the 20 s ping_interval.
6. Not Python-version dependent (an unbounded await on a never-completed Future); I ran 3.13 only.
7. For A11.4, the overrun is at most click_delay plus one check_input; with the defaults and an immediate find it is about 0.03 s.
8. For A5.7, the busy spin is limited by the timeout; the real bug is that timeout<=0 makes zero attempts.
9. Each realism rating: the main hang is medium (pages with load or timer alerts are uncommon but real, and #77/#291 shows users hit the same thing in wait_for_ready_state), A5.7 is low-medium, A11.4 is low.

groups.summary: Reproduced every member with my own probes, on real headless Chromium 141 and on a browser-free fake CDP peer. (1) Browser._stop awaits Target.detachFromTarget (inside Connection.aclose, connection.py:517) and Browser.close (browser.py:883), and neither has a timeout. A frozen or unresponsive browser therefore makes stop() hang forever before it reaches terminate/kill. Bounding stop() with wait_for leaves the process alive and the profile on disk, and the atexit hook has already been unregistered, so nothing cleans up later. (2) If Chrome dies just before stop(), Connection.aclose raises ConnectionClosedError, because it only catches ProtocolException. The exception aborts _stop: _process stays set, the process is never reaped and the profile leaks. (3) Two concurrent stop() calls race in the terminate/poll loop and one raises AttributeError 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'poll' at _stop:901. (4) Under asyncio.run, the atexit cleanup always fails at `await asyncio.to_thread(self._process.wait)` (_stop:909) with RuntimeError('Executor shutdown has been called'), so the /tmp/uc_* profile leaks. This happens on Python 3.13 and 3.11, and also on the Ctrl+C path. Tab.close() also hangs well past the 10 s its docstring promises, stuck at Tab.close:1079 -> Connection.send.

fix_assessment.diff_summary: zendriver/core/browser.py only (full diff in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-zendriver/b2021b39-94e6-5220-9e66-7f33c0314a80/scratchpad/verify/Q3-fixsafety/fix.diff). (a) New module constant STOP_COMMAND_TIMEOUT = 5 (could be private). (b) _stop: replace `for target in self.targets: await target.aclose()` with `await asyncio.wait_for(asyncio.gather(*(t.aclose() for t in self.targets), return_exceptions=True), STOP_COMMAND_TIMEOUT)` inside `except asyncio.TimeoutError: logger.debug(...)`. This gives one budget for all targets, and per-target exceptions such as ConnectionClosedError are swallowed. (c) Wrap the Browser.close send in asyncio.wait_for(..., STOP_COMMAND_TIMEOUT); the existing broad except already covers the timeout. (d) Snapshot `process = self._process` and use the local for terminate/poll/kill, so a concurrent stop() setting self._process=None cannot break this one. (e) Remove `await asyncio.to_thread(self._process.wait)`: the break path is already reaped by poll(), and after kill() it uses `while process.poll() is None: await asyncio.sleep(0.05)`, which needs no default executor. (f) stop(): call `await self._stop()` first, then asyncio_atexit.unregister and registry discard, so a stop() that fails or is cancelled keeps the atexit fallback.
fix_assessment.risks: No locks are added, so there are no re-entrancy, deadlock or lock-ordering concerns. Cancellation still propagates: wait_for/gather re-raise CancelledError. Each aclose calls _detach_session() synchronously before its send, so a timeout leaves local session state consistent, and Connection.aclose() later fails or clears any pending browser-connection transactions. Behaviour changes callers would notice: (1) stop() of a hung browser now returns after about 23 s with a 'Could not send the close command' warning instead of hanging; (2) detaches run concurrently rather than one after another; (3) gather(return_exceptions=True) drops exceptions other than ProtocolException from aclose without logging them (suggest debug-logging the results); (4) after a stop() that fails or is cancelled, the atexit callback and its strong reference to the Browser stay until loop close, where _atexit_cleanup retries. That is intended, but it is new. (5) A slow but healthy Chrome that takes more than 5 s to answer Browser.close now gets terminate() early. On POSIX that is a graceful SIGTERM. On Windows terminate() is TerminateProcess, but it was already called right after the reply, so this is no worse. The post-kill poll loop is unbounded, like the old wait() (only matters for a D-state process). Python 3.10 compatibility: only wait_for, gather and asyncio.TimeoutError are used. I tested 3.13 and 3.11, not 3.10. Healthy-path stop time is unchanged (0.37 s), and the repo's test_browser_stop_exits_gracefully_without_kill still passes.

fix_assessment.risks:
(a) The triage hypothesis, a strict asyncio.wait_for(loop, timeout) as in #291, is unsafe as written:
- wait_for(..., <=0) never runs the attempt. That breaks timeout=0 one-shot checks, and xpath's internal find_all(xpath, timeout=0) would then always return [].
- It cuts the trailing 0.5 s sleep, so the last attempt is lost. Confirmed on Chromium: elements appearing 0.3 s into timeout=0.5, or 0.7 s into timeout=1, are found by the repo but get TimeoutError with the strict wrap.
- wait_for's sleep after a hit gets cut, so an element it already found is discarded.
The prototype avoids all three with the timeout<=0 bypass, a grace of one poll interval, clamped sleeps and no sleep after a hit.
(b) The companion fix in Connection._register_handlers is required. Without it, a pending domain enable (a handler registered while the page is blocked) makes the call hang and become uncancellable, and the same applies to the existing wait_for_ready_state fix.
(c) Behaviour changes callers may notice:
- A blocked page now raises or returns at timeout+0.5 s instead of hanging.
- wait_for and tab() return as soon as the element is found (no 0.5 s trailing sleep) and give up at about timeout instead of timeout+0.5.
- The last find/select attempt happens at the deadline instead of up to 0.5 s after it.
- xpath polls every 0.5 s instead of spinning (13 vs 1272 sends in 0.5 s), so an element can be found up to 0.5 s later. timeout<=0 now makes one attempt and can return elements where it used to return [].
- verify_cf's click_delay sleeps are clamped to the deadline, so solves that were only detected after the deadline now raise TimeoutError, as the docstring says they should.
(d) timeout<=0 deliberately keeps one unbounded attempt, so it still hangs on a blocked renderer, as query_selector does.
(e) Cancellation side effects (the same as with #291):
- xpath cancelled between DOM.enable and disable leaves the DOM agent enabled.
- A cancelled performSearch leaves a search session open in the browser.
- A cancelled Transaction stays in mapper until Chrome replies (verified it drains once the dialog is dismissed).
- A cancelled first-time _attach_session can leak a browser-side session.
(f) No lock is held across the bounded region. _open_lock and _attach_lock are released by `async with` on cancel, and the helper takes no lock, so there is no re-entrancy or deadlock issue. Nested calls are fine: xpath calls find_all(timeout=0) from inside its bounded poll.
(g) Builtin vs asyncio TimeoutError: on 3.10 they differ. verify_cf converts explicitly, and the tab methods keep asyncio.TimeoutError. Verified on 3.10.20, 3.11.17 and 3.13.16.
(h) The 0.5 s grace is a heuristic. A final attempt that takes longer than 0.5 s on a very heavy page is cut, giving TimeoutError where the repo would have returned the result.

groups.refinements: 1) Attach mode (host+port given): the triage hypothesis, plain stop() then re-raise, is unsafe. _stop sends cdp.browser.close() whenever the connection is open, so a failed attach would close the user's existing browser. I checked this with a variant prototype: test_failed_attach_does_not_close_the_existing_browser fails with `'Browser.close' in ['Target.setDiscoverTargets','Browser.close']`. The prototype closes only the connection when connect_existing. 2) Remaining gap, also present before the fix: _stop returns early when there is neither a connection nor a process (`if not self.connection and not self._process: return`), skipping _cleanup_temporary_profile. In attach mode, a cancel before the connection exists still leaves the empty uc_* dir that self.config() created via mkdtemp (verified: registry 0 but the temp dir exists on the prototype). A failure in _start_process itself also leaks that dir. Both are minor and outside the 'after Chrome is spawned' claim. 3) A second cancel arriving during cleanup interrupts stop() in its terminate/sleep loop: the process was already SIGTERMed (poll -15) and unregistered, but the profile is left. That is still much better than before (process alive, registered=1). 4) coro.close()/GeneratorExit while start() is suspended now raises RuntimeError('coroutine ignored GeneratorExit'); the process still gets SIGTERM. Before the fix close() succeeded silently and leaked the process. This happens only for start() coroutines that are closed or garbage-collected without being cancelled. 5) Suggested hardening: wrap the cleanup in `try: ... except Exception: logger.debug(..., exc_info=True)`, so an error raised inside stop() cannot replace the original exception. Replacing a CancelledError would turn wait_for's TimeoutError into that error.

fix_assessment.diff_summary: zendriver/core/browser.py, Browser.start: after `util.get_registered_instances().add(self)`, the rest of start() moves unchanged into a new `async def _connect(self, connect_existing: bool) -> None` (its trailing `return self` is removed). start() now does `try: await self._connect(connect_existing) except BaseException: if connect_existing and self.connection: await self.connection.aclose()  # do not close a browser that was not launched here; await self.stop(); raise` and then `return self`. stop() is idempotent: the second call made after the existing 'Failed to connect' path returns early, and asyncio_atexit.unregister of a callback that was never registered is a no-op. Browser.create is unchanged.
fix_assessment.risks: No locks are on the start/stop path (_update_target_info_mutex is used only in _handle_target_update), so there is no re-entrancy or lock-ordering risk. Behaviour changes callers would notice: (a) wait_for(zd.start(), T) now raises only after cleanup completes, about 0.25s later with a Chrome that honours SIGTERM (measured T=0.05 gave 0.30s; 3s hangs gave 3.3-3.4s), and up to about 3s more plus kill if Chrome ignores SIGTERM. (b) A Chrome launched by zendriver gets Browser.close on a failed start. (c) In attach mode the connection is closed but the remote browser is left running, and the instance is unregistered. (d) A user who calls `await browser.start()` directly and handles the failure gets an already-stopped instance; calling stop() again is a harmless no-op, and start() can be retried because _process is cleared. Residual risks: a second cancel during cleanup leaves the temp profile (the process is already SIGTERMed); an exception raised inside stop() would replace the original exception or CancelledError (suggest suppressing Exception from the cleanup with a debug log); GeneratorExit via coro.close() now produces RuntimeError('coroutine ignored GeneratorExit'); in attach mode a cancel before the connection exists still leaves an empty uc_* temp dir because of _stop's early return. Verified on Python 3.13 and 3.11.
